### P1: background eval `judge()` and `find` outlive the permitted foreground turn

The exclusions are **not valid as blanket exclusions**.

I ran real primary HTTP turns that invoked the production EvalTool and JavaScript worker. The eval either backgrounded a `judge()`/`tool.find()` call or returned a detached `judgeBatch()` handle. The primary turn then finished. Only afterward did I begin disposal and release the held judge credential.

The endpoint received:

| Producer | Live control | After `beginDispose()` | During actual `dispose()` shutdown-hook wait |
|---|---|---|---|
| Background eval `judge()` | `[false]` | `[true]` | `[true]` |
| Background eval `find` | `[false,false]` | `[true,true]` | `[true,true]` |
| Detached `judgeBatch()` | `[false]` | `[true]` | `[true]` |

Each value is `session.isDisposed` when the HTTP request arrived. In all nine cases, `session.prompt()` had already resolved and `isStreaming` was false.

Relevant files:

- `tools/eval.ts:593–720` moves work onto the background job’s signal.
- `eval/judgment-bridge.ts:238–287` and `tools/jfind/index.ts:100–123` use tool cancellation, without a disposal owner.
- `eval/judgment-batch-bridge.ts:213–250,365–428` deliberately starts work that outlives its cell.
- `session/agent-session.ts:6288–6304,6413–6458` cancels owned jobs/batches later, after shutdown hooks and other waits—not at `beginDispose()`.

Final real-turn matrix: **6 pass / 6 fail**. All six failures are late-request assertions. The passing cases include three live controls, prelude reentrancy, and two foreground controls.

Those foreground controls establish the needed distinction: ordinary foreground `find`, and even a floated JavaScript `judge()` promise, remain owned by the admitted turn and may finish. Backgrounded or detached work does not.

**Fix the ownership distinction, not individual helper names:** cancel detached/background model work at `beginDispose()` while preserving genuinely foreground work.

finder_sections.text:
### P1 — the seven opt-outs permit continued inference during teardown

Preserving park/detach/tombstone decisions is justified. Continuing provider execution while waiting to make those decisions is broader than that requirement.

I measured the common registration boundary with seven real provider-driving agents, the real `ExtensionRunner`, and an ordinary non-opted control:

| Case | Cancellation window | New credentialed requests across seven jobs | Ordinary control |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Immediate disposal | 3.94–4.18 ms | 0 | 0 |
| One stuck shutdown handler | 2,014.00–2,014.49 ms | **613** | 0 |
| Three stuck shutdown handlers | 2,017.30–2,018.26 ms | **796** | 0 |
| Explicit 750-ms `beginDispose()` wrapper gap | 752.55–753.60 ms | **388** | 0 |

The endpoint used a controlled 5-ms response delay. These are measured possible counts, not typical cloud-provider throughput. `beginDispose()` itself imposes no deadline on the wrapper gap.

**Coverage boundary:** this exercises all seven registrations’ shared cancellation mechanism, not seven complete frontend launch paths.

A widget for an opted-out job also sends a disposed request; the ordinary-job widget sends none. That UI request needs no lifecycle exception.
